key_items: The package updates EU rules for payment services by replacing the current PSD2 framework and amending older settlement provisions, shifting from a directive-only approach to a broader set of harmonised obligations across the internal market.

The document is an EESC opinion on the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR) review, assessing how disclosure rules should be adjusted to improve clarity, comparability and credibility of sustainability-related claims by financial market participants.

Updates the Eurosystem’s rules for managing collateral in ECB credit operations, clarifying how eligible assets are handled, valued and mobilised, and setting out operational requirements for counterparties.

Updates the ECB’s 2014 framework for “additional temporary measures” in Eurosystem refinancing, including rules on what collateral is eligible for central-bank credit, and it amends the earlier collateral/refinancing guideline (recast of ECB/2007/9).

title: EUR-Lex Daily Digest — 2026-04-05
key_items: François-Louis Michaud's appointment as Chair of the European Banking Authority (EBA) marks a significant leadership change that will influence the direction of EU banking regulation and oversight starting April 16, 2026.
The final report outlines updated supervisory reporting and public disclosure requirements under Solvency II, aiming to enhance transparency and consistency in the insurance sector across the EU.

abstract: Today's European policy briefing underscores a pivotal moment in the regulatory landscape, particularly within the banking and insurance sectors, while also addressing the broader implications of climate change on financial stability. The appointment of François-Louis Michaud as Chair of the European Banking Authority (EBA), effective April 16, 2026, signals a forthcoming shift in EU banking regulation. Michaud's leadership is anticipated to recalibrate the EBA's focus on financial stability and consumer protection, potentially altering the regulatory priorities that govern banks across the EU. This transition period allows for strategic preparation, especially as the banking sector faces evolving economic challenges and regulatory demands [1]. In parallel, the final report on Solvency II introduces updated supervisory reporting and public disclosure requirements aimed at enhancing transparency in the insurance sector. By streamlining reporting processes and improving data quality, the revisions seek to alleviate administrative burdens while bolstering stakeholder confidence. This initiative is crucial for fostering better risk management practices within insurance companies, which are increasingly vital in a climate-affected economic environment [2].

title: EUR-Lex Daily Digest — 2025-11-27
key_items: EIOPA Pensions Techsprint 2025 - Post-event Report

The European Banking Authority (EBA) today published a Peer Review assessing how effectively supervisors implement and supervise diversity policies, specifically gender diversity, within the management bodies of financial institutions.

The European Banking Authority (EBA) today published its semi-annual dashboard on the minimum requirement for own funds and eligible liabilities (MREL), which updates the information on the state of resolution planning and on the resources that banks are using to meet the requirements.
Trade turmoil in April 2025 saw a marked change in cross-asset behaviour compared with typical patterns.
Financial stability vulnerabilities remain elevated given uncertainty over geoeconomic trends and tariffs impact

title: EUR-Lex Daily Digest — 2025-10-17
key_items: The new Regulation (EU) 2025/1958 updates reporting requirements for supervisory financial information under Regulation (EU) 2015/534.
The Council Decision (EU) 2025/2126 authorizes the EU to sign an Amending Protocol with San Marino regarding automatic financial account information exchange.
The Council Decision (EU) 2025/2124 amends the existing agreement on automatic exchange of financial account information between the EU and Liechtenstein.
The Council Decision (EU) 2025/2120 authorizes the EU to sign an Amending Protocol with Andorra regarding automatic financial account information exchange.
The Council Decision (EU) 2025/2125 authorizes the EU to sign an Amending Protocol with Monaco regarding financial account information exchange.
abstract: The items [1] to [5] reflect significant regulatory developments within the European Union aimed at enhancing financial reporting and international tax compliance. Item [1] introduces Regulation (EU) 2025/1958, which updates supervisory financial reporting requirements, expanding the scope to include more financial institutions and mandating more frequent and detailed submissions. This regulation aims to improve compliance with supervisory standards by requiring institutions to adapt their reporting processes by January 1, 2026. Items [2] to [5] involve Council Decisions authorizing the EU to sign Amending Protocols with San Marino, Liechtenstein, Andorra, and Monaco. These protocols focus on the automatic exchange of financial account information to bolster international tax compliance. Each protocol enhances existing agreements by expanding the scope of data shared and imposing stricter reporting obligations on financial institutions. The implementation timelines for these protocols are set for 2026, aligning with international standards.

abstract: The key themes across the items [1] to [4] revolve around the legal authority and operational robustness of the Single Resolution Mechanism (SRM) in managing banking crises, particularly in the context of the resolution scheme for Banco Popular Español. The General Court's orders consistently dismissed annulment actions from various parties, citing a manifest lack of legal foundation and, in some cases, a lack of jurisdiction. This reinforces the SRM's role and the legal framework governing credit institutions and investment firms, indicating that affected stakeholders must comply with the SRM's resolution measures. The implications of these rulings suggest a strong judicial endorsement of the SRM's authority, which may deter future legal challenges against its decisions. The decisions also clarify the scope of judicial review available under the SRM, emphasizing the need for substantial legal grounds in any future actions. In contrast, item [5] discusses the Commission's amendment of the Guidelines on State aid for rescuing and restructuring non-financial undertakings, extending the application period and broadening eligibility criteria. abstract: The key themes across the items can be categorized into macroeconomic heterogeneity and regulatory compliance in financial contexts. 1. Macroeconomic Heterogeneity: Items [1] and [2] emphasize the significance of household and firm-level heterogeneity in understanding the effects of monetary policy in the euro area. Research indicates that monetary policy easing can temporarily reduce consumption inequality among households, highlighting the need for policymakers to consider these disparities when designing economic strategies. While household heterogeneity provides new insights, it does not fundamentally alter the understanding of overall economic dynamics, unlike firm-level heterogeneity, which remains valuable for forecasting aggregate economic variables. 2. Macroeconomic Impacts of Defense Spending: Item [3] discusses the implications of increased defense spending in the euro area, revealing low government purchase multipliers and potential inflationary pressures. The analysis underscores the importance of considering distributional effects and the varying impacts on consumption across different wealth levels, suggesting that fiscal policies must account for these disparities to avoid unintended consequences.

abstract: The key themes across the items revolve around the enforcement of rights and obligations under EU law, particularly concerning data protection and employment regulations. In the context of data protection, as highlighted in [1], [2], and [3], the Court's judgment clarifies the scope of the right to erasure and restriction of processing under GDPR Articles 17 and 18. It emphasizes the right to effective judicial remedies for individuals whose data has been unlawfully processed, reinforcing the importance of accountability for data controllers. The concept of 'non-material damage' is significant in compensation claims, with the controller's degree of fault potentially influencing compensation assessments. This underscores the necessity for data controllers to comply with GDPR provisions to avoid legal repercussions. In employment law, as discussed in [4], the Court addresses the principle of non-discrimination in fixed-term work agreements, particularly for judiciary members. It clarifies obligations regarding equal treatment and the right to paid annual leave, impacting those transitioning from fixed-term to permanent roles. The ruling establishes a timeline for assessment procedures that affect claims to accrued leave, highlighting the procedural complexities involved.

abstract: The key themes across the items [1], [2], and [3] focus on the EFTA Surveillance Authority's recommendation regarding ex ante regulation in the electronic communications sector, aligned with the European Electronic Communications Code (Directive (EU) 2018/1972). The recommendations identify specific product and service markets that will be subject to new regulatory obligations, impacting telecommunications providers and service operators within the EEA. The effective date of April 9, 2025, marks a significant timeline for compliance, necessitating that stakeholders assess their operations against the new framework. In contrast, items [4] and [5] discuss advancements in econometric analysis, specifically in Bayesian structural vector autoregressions (VAR). They highlight the inadequacy of conventional pointwise quantiles in capturing uncertainty in impulse responses and propose new joint inference methods that yield wider error bands. These methods are shown to enhance the robustness of economic forecasts, particularly for inflation and GDP, by providing more reliable estimates of fiscal multipliers. The implications of these findings suggest a need for regulatory adaptation in the electronic communications sector while also advocating for improved methodologies in economic analysis to ensure accurate forecasting and robust decision-making.
